steps.prompt: Which sentence would help you find the lost dog?
steps.b: After the storm, the dog was sleeping under the porch of the yellow house.
steps.reveal: Three prepositional phrases (after the storm, under the porch, of the yellow house) answer when, where and which. They turn a vague sentence into a useful one.

cards.title: Preposition + object = phrase
cards.body: A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition and ends with its noun or pronoun, plus any words that describe it: in the box, behind the old shed, with my best friend, for them. The phrase works as one unit.

cards.title: What phrases do
cards.body: Some phrases describe a noun, like an adjective: “the girl with the red umbrella” (which girl?). Others describe a verb, like an adverb: “she waited at the station” (where?), “we left after dinner” (when?).

cards.title: Start with a phrase
cards.text:
We played soccer after school. → After school, we played soccer.
A red bench stands behind the gym. → Behind the gym, a red bench stands.
cards.note: Moving a phrase to the front varies your sentence openings. Put a comma after it.

cards.title: Phrases and agreement
cards.text:
The box of crayons IS on the shelf.
The players on the team ARE tired.
cards.note: The subject is never inside a prepositional phrase. Cover the phrase to find it.

prompts: Which of your phrases would help your friend most? Why?
How does starting a sentence with a phrase change how your writing sounds?
